questions.q: How does a Sensor differ from a regular Operator task?
options: It cannot fail under any circumstances
It checks a condition repeatedly on an interval, succeeding only once that condition becomes true
It skips the scheduler entirely
It runs faster than any other task type
questions.explain: A Sensor waits and repeatedly checks a condition, unlike a normal Operator that runs once and finishes.

questions.q: What does `mode="reschedule"` do for a Sensor?
options: Makes the Sensor check twice as often
Converts the Sensor into a regular Operator
Frees the worker slot between checks, instead of holding it for the entire wait
Disables the timeout entirely
questions.explain: reschedule mode releases the worker between checks — much better than poke mode for long waits, which would otherwise tie up a worker doing nothing.

A specific task (or DAG) in a different DAG to reach a given state
The Airflow scheduler to restart
A file to appear in a local directory only
questions.explain: ExternalTaskSensor is the standard way to chain two independently-scheduled DAGs by waiting on a task/DAG in another DAG.

questions.q: According to this lesson, how does a Sensor appear in the Grid and Graph views?
options: Like any other task — it participates in dependencies, retries, and trigger rules the same way
It's invisible until it succeeds
It appears in a completely separate, dedicated view
It cannot be viewed in the UI at all
questions.explain: A Sensor is still just a task under the hood — the only real difference is what its execute() method does internally.

questions.q: What does `timeout` control on a Sensor?
options: How long the Sensor keeps checking before failing the task
How many workers are assigned to the Sensor
The DAG's overall schedule interval
How many retries the Sensor gets after succeeding
questions.explain: timeout sets the maximum time the Sensor will keep checking its condition before giving up and failing.
